meta.name: Dog Years to Human Years: A Chart by Size, and What the Number Means
meta.title_tag: Dog Years to Human Years: Chart by Size + Formula
meta.excerpt: There's no exact conversion. The vet chart most sources use counts a dog's first year as about 15 human years and the second as about 9 more, then adds roughly 4 to 7 years per birthday depending on size. Here's the full chart, the newer DNA-based formula, and when your dog becomes a senior.
meta.meta_description: Convert your dog's age to human years with a size-based chart and the DNA-based formula, then see when your dog counts as a senior and what changes then.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Senior Labrador Retriever with a grey muzzle — how dog years translate into human years depends on size

body_html:
Quick Answer: There's no exact conversion, and "multiply by 7" is a myth (AVMA). The common vet chart counts a dog's first year as about 15 human years and the second as about 9 more, then adds roughly 4 years per birthday for small dogs, 4–5 for medium, 5–6 for large and about 7 for giant breeds (AVMA, AKC). A 2020 DNA study of Labradors gives different numbers. For your dog's care, life stage matters more: vets count the last 25% of expected lifespan as "senior" (AAHA), from about 6–7 years in giant breeds to 8–11 in small ones (AVMA). See the chart ↓

Dog Years to Human Years Chart by Size

Find your dog's age on the left and their adult weight across the top. The medium column is the AVMA's chart for dogs weighing 21–50 pounds. The small, large and giant columns come from the American Kennel Club's chart, whose medium column matches the AVMA's exactly. The last column is our own calculation from a 2020 DNA study of Labradors (explained below).

All of these are approximations; the AVMA's chart itself says to ask your veterinarian. We stopped the large column at 14 and the giant column at 12, where the AKC's figures reach about 90. The AKC chart keeps adding years in a straight line, so a 16-year-old giant comes out at 121. Weight cutoffs vary too: the AKC splits large from giant at 100 pounds, the AVMA's senior guidance at 90. For a mixed breed, go by adult weight, or check our dog breeds by size guide.

Giant breeds start a little lower, then overtake every other size by age three. After that, small dogs add about 4 human years per birthday, medium dogs 4–5, large dogs 5–6 and giants about 7.

Why "Multiply by 7" Is Wrong

The AVMA is direct: "Contrary to popular belief, dogs do not age at a rate of 7 human years per dog year." The rule's origin is unclear; the AKC describes the usual explanation, simple arithmetic from people living about 70 years and dogs about 10.

It fails at both ends of life. Puppies rush through childhood: rapid growth ends at about 6–9 months, and some small-breed females have their first heat at 4 months (AAHA). A 1-year-old dog is not a 7-year-old child. Later, size takes over: at age 10 the chart puts a small dog at 56 and a giant at 79, a spread no single multiplier captures. The DNA study found the same shape, with fast change in puppies that "slows markedly in canine adulthood" (Wang et al.).

The DNA "Epigenetic Clock" Formula, Explained

In 2020, a UC San Diego team led by Trey Ideker compared methylation, chemical tags on DNA that shift predictably with age, in blood from 104 dogs and 320 people. The dogs were almost all Labrador Retrievers, from a few weeks to 16 years old. Matching each dog to the people with the most similar patterns produced this formula (Wang et al., Cell Systems):

human age = 16 × ln(dog age) + 31

"ln" is the natural logarithm key on any scientific calculator, including most phone calculators. For a 4-year-old dog: ln(4) is about 1.39, times 16 is about 22, plus 31 is about 53.

The formula lined up with real milestones: an 8-week-old puppy matched a baby of about 9 months, a stage when both are cutting their first teeth, and the typical Labrador lifespan of 12 years translated to 70, the worldwide human life expectancy. The authors spell out its limits:

  • One breed. The study "focused exclusively on Labrador retrievers," and other breeds "could yield different age-translation functions."
  • Blood only. The makeup of blood cells itself shifts with age.
  • Rough in the middle years. For adolescent and adult dogs, "the correspondence was more approximate," with dogs' DNA changing faster than their physical milestones would suggest.

It also disagrees with the chart. It makes a 1-year-old dog 31 (chart: 15) and a 3-year-old 49 (chart: 28), then flattens, putting every dog from 11 to 16 between 69 and 75. Both come from credible sources, so treat each as a rough translation. The AAHA's life stage guidelines skip human-age equivalents entirely and define stages by age and characteristics instead.

Why Big Dogs Age Faster

Across mammal species, bigger usually means longer-lived; within dogs it's the reverse. Analyzing death records from 74 breeds, Kraus and colleagues found no clear link between size and when aging begins. The difference was pace: "large dogs die young mainly because they age quickly." Summarizing this research, the AKC puts the cost at about a month of life expectancy for every 4.4 pounds of body mass.

In UK records on 584,734 dogs, median lifespan was 12.5 years. Purebreds lived a median 12.7 years if small, 12.5 if medium and 11.9 if large. Flat-faced purebreds had a median of 11.2, and small, long-nosed breeds lived longest, with a median of 13.3 years for females (McMillan 2024). US clinic records on 13.3 million dogs put life expectancy at birth at 12.7 years, rising as size fell (Montoya 2023, by Royal Canin and Banfield researchers; both companies are owned by Mars). See our longest-living dog breeds and healthiest dog breeds guides for breed numbers, or giant dog breeds if you live with a big one.

When Is a Dog a Senior?

There's no single birthday. The AAHA's senior care guidelines say "there is no specific age for senior status" and define a senior as a dog in "the last 25% of estimated lifespan through end of life." For a breed that usually lives about 12 years, that starts around 9. The AVMA's typical ages by adult weight:

  • Small or toy (under 20 lb): 8–11 years
  • Medium (20–50 lb): 8–10 years
  • Large (50–90 lb): 8–9 years
  • Giant (over 90 lb): 6–7 years

Sources draw the lines slightly differently: the AKC puts small breeds at 8–12 and notes that vets often start suggesting twice-yearly visits around 7. As one veterinarian told the AKC, a 9-year-old Great Dane is typically much more senior than a 9-year-old Chihuahua. For a mixed breed, use adult weight and ask your vet.

What Changes at Each Life Stage

The AAHA divides a dog's life into five stages. Ages and visit frequencies below are from its guidelines unless noted.

StageTypical ageWhat to expectVet visits
PuppyBirth to about 6–9 months (large breeds often grow until 9–15 months)Rapid growth; all 42 adult teeth by 7 months (Merck)Frequent visits for vaccines and prevention
Young adultTo 3–4 yearsPhysical and social maturityEvery 6–12 months
Mature adultUntil the last 25% of expected lifespanArthritis and weight gain can start quietly; cognitive testing has found memory decline starting at 6–8 years (Merck)Every 6–12 months, plus yearly baseline tests
SeniorLast 25% of expected lifespanMore heart, kidney and liver disease, diabetes, joint disease, vision or hearing loss, cancer and cognitive decline (AVMA)At least twice a year; blood and urine tests every 6–12 months
End of lifeVariesComfort and quality of life come firstAs needed, including an honest quality-of-life review (AVMA)

When to start senior checkups: as soon as your dog enters the senior range above, move to exams at least twice a year (AAHA, AVMA), with a blood count, chemistry panel and urinalysis every 6–12 months (AAHA 2023). Cancer causes almost half of deaths in dogs over 10 (AVMA), so have any new lump checked by your vet promptly rather than waiting to see if it grows. Age itself isn't a disease (AVMA), so new confusion, house soiling or sudden weight loss call for a vet visit.

Three things are worth starting earlier:

  • Look for arthritis early. In an NC State study of 123 dogs aged 8 months to 4 years, 39.8% had X-ray signs of osteoarthritis in at least one joint, and owners noticed problems in only about 30% of the dogs with painful arthritis (Enomoto 2024; three authors disclosed ties to the drug company Elanco). Tell your vet if your dog walks stiffly, struggles to stand, or starts avoiding stairs, jumps or car rides (AVMA). See our guide to helping a dog with arthritis at home.
  • Keep your dog lean. In a lifelong Purina study of 48 Labradors, dogs fed 25% less than their pair-mates lived a median 13.0 years, against 11.2 for the other dogs, which were all overweight (Kealy 2002; Penn Today). In US clinic records, obese dogs' life expectancy was 11.7 years, against 13.2 at ideal weight (Montoya 2023). Ask your vet for a target weight; green beans make a low-calorie treat.
  • Watch the mind from about 7. Guidelines from the CCDS Working Group (JAVMA, December 2025) call for yearly cognitive screening from age 7, and a detailed cognitive questionnaire every 6 months for all dogs from 10 (NC State). Our dog dementia guide covers the signs.

How to Estimate an Adopted Dog's Age

Puppies are easier, because teeth come in on a fairly predictable schedule: baby teeth arrive at 3–5 weeks, adult teeth start at about 4–5 months, and all 42 are in by 7 months (Merck). Even so, Merck calls tooth-based aging of young dogs only "somewhat accurate."

Adults are harder. Merck says vets can estimate age from tooth wear in most large adult dogs, but it's more difficult in small and toy breeds. In a German study of 295 dogs, combining eye-lens reflection, tooth wear and tartar still left a standard error of about 2.26 years, and the authors called age estimation in dogs "very crude" (Gesierich 2015). A shelter's "about 5" could be two or more years off either way, so ask your vet whether to start senior checkups at the younger end of the range.

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian. This guide summarizes the veterinary sources and studies listed below and isn't a substitute for advice from your vet.

Frequently Asked Questions

How old is a 10-year-old dog in human years?

About 56 for a small dog, 60 for a medium dog, 66 for a large dog and 79 for a giant breed on the AVMA and AKC charts, or about 68 by the 2020 DNA formula built on Labradors. Both are estimates. Most 10-year-old dogs are seniors or close to it, so twice-yearly checkups make sense (AVMA).

Is one dog year really equal to seven human years?

No, the AVMA calls that a popular belief that doesn't hold. Dogs age fastest in their first two years (about 24 human years by age two), then more slowly, and big dogs age faster than small ones.

At what age is my dog considered a senior?

In the last 25% of their expected lifespan (AAHA). The AVMA's typical ages are 8–11 for small dogs, 8–10 for medium, 8–9 for large and 6–7 for giant breeds. Your vet can estimate where your dog falls.

Why do small dogs live longer than big dogs?

Big dogs seem to age faster rather than start aging earlier (Kraus 2013). In UK records on more than half a million dogs, small purebreds lived a median 12.7 years and large purebreds 11.9 (McMillan 2024).

How can I tell how old my rescue dog is?

Puppies are easier, because teeth erupt on a fairly predictable schedule and all 42 adult teeth are in by 7 months (Merck). For adults, an estimate from the teeth and eyes can be off by two years or more (Gesierich 2015), so treat it as a range.

How long do dogs usually live?

About 12.7 years from birth in US clinic records (Montoya 2023) and a median of 12.5 years in UK records (McMillan 2024). Small, long-nosed breeds tend to live longest; large and flat-faced breeds, shorter.
